terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: Cuts a plaintiff's award by the share of fault assigned to them — a pure system pays even a plaintiff who is 90% at fault, while a modified system bars recovery once fault reaches 50% or 51%. The older contributory-negligence rule, still law in a few states, denies any recovery at all to a plaintiff who is even 1% at fault, and that all-or-nothing contrast is what exam items are actually testing.
terms.whyItMatters: A slip-and-fall damages question gives $100,000 in harm and 30% plaintiff fault and asks what the business actually pays.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.

terms.definition: Sellers must re-scrub their calling lists against the federal registry at least every 31 days, and may reach a listed consumer only through an existing business relationship — 18 months after that person's last purchase, or 3 months after an inquiry — or with signed written permission. A list bought once and used for a year fails the scrub requirement no matter how it was sourced.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a purchase date and a call date and ask whether the relationship exemption still covers the call; a prospecting roleplay is scored on saying how often the list is cleaned.

terms.definition: The Consumer Product Safety Act duty to notify the Commission within 24 hours of obtaining information that a product contains a defect creating a substantial hazard, fails a mandatory standard, or poses an unreasonable risk -- and the duty applies even when the firm still disputes the defect.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and consumer-protection roleplays test whether you report before finishing your own investigation; waiting for certainty is the answer that loses the indicator and, in practice, draws the fine.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Any contact at which a buyer forms a judgment about a brand with no marketing message present to help — Procter & Gamble named the 3 to 7 seconds facing the shelf the first such moment and the first use of the product the second; the practical rule is that advertising spend cannot repair a touchpoint at which the customer has already decided against the brand.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about check-in or complaint handling are scored on identifying the exact contact that decides the guest's opinion and fixing that, not on adding promotion.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of how threatened a culture feels by ambiguity, which predicts how much written structure a message must carry: high scorers such as Greece near 100 and Japan near 92 expect detailed agendas, explicit rules and signed detail before acting, while low scorers such as Singapore near 8 and Denmark near 23 will work from an open-ended proposal. It is not risk aversion in the financial sense - a high-scoring culture may take a very large risk, provided the procedure for taking it is spelled out.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to prepare for a first meeting with a Japanese partner is scored on sending the agenda and documentation in advance rather than planning to improvise.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: Total pay a rep receives at exactly 100% of quota — base salary plus variable pay at plan, so a $60,000 base with $60,000 of commission at plan is $120,000 at a 50/50 pay mix. It is a plan figure and not a promise: only the base half is paid regardless of results, which is what separates it from a salary.
terms.whyItMatters: A recruiting roleplay that pitches a sales job is scored on explaining the split honestly, and quoting the total as if it were guaranteed is an ethical mark against you.

terms.definition: Nothing can be inspected, weighed, or returned before purchase, so buyers judge search qualities beforehand, experience qualities only during delivery, and credence qualities -- a surgeon's technique, a tax opinion -- never at all; a good lets buyers verify most attributes before paying.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay contrasting service marketing with product marketing is scored on the tangible cues you add -- uniforms, facilities, guarantees -- to stand in for inspection.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: Short for best alternative to a negotiated agreement: the course of action you would actually take if these talks failed, which is what sets real bargaining power. It is not the price target and not the reservation price — the reservation price is the worst deal still worth accepting, derived from the alternative — and improving the outside option raises your power even if nothing at the table changes.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier or salary negotiation roleplay is scored on the candidate knowing their walk-away option and estimating the other side's before conceding.

terms.definition: Moore's gap between the 13.5% early-adopter band, which buys on the promise of a breakthrough and tolerates an incomplete product, and the 34% early majority, which buys only on references from people already like themselves; products stall in it because the two groups will not act as references for each other, and the standard bridge is dominating one narrow beachhead segment until its references become credible to the next group.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay shows strong early sales that suddenly flatten, naming this gap and the beachhead fix is the diagnosis a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring prior express written consent — signed, specific to marketing contact, and not made a condition of buying anything — before an autodialer or prerecorded message may call or text a mobile number, and requiring every seller to keep its own internal do-not-call list for five years. A checkbox buried in a purchase flow does not meet the standard.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-selling roleplay on texting a prospect list is graded on whether you ask how consent was captured; exam items contrast a consumer who bought something with one who signed a marketing permission.

terms.definition: A label a written warranty may carry only if it repairs defects free within a reasonable time, puts no duty on the buyer beyond giving notice, does not limit the duration of implied warranties, and offers a refund or replacement after a reasonable number of failed repairs; missing any one forces the 'limited' label.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty roleplays ask what a store may print on the tag; a written warranty that charges a handling fee cannot be called full, and knowing which of the four conditions broke is the scoring point.

terms.definition: The total annualized return on a bond held to the end of its term, counting coupon payments plus any gain or loss between purchase price and face value.
terms.whyItMatters: A bond bought below face value returns more than its stated coupon rate, and this is the figure that shows it in an investment comparison.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: The number-two or number-three firm by share — roughly 30% against a leader's 40% in Kotler's benchmark structure, above a follower's 20% and a nicher's 10% — which attacks the leader or smaller rivals head-on rather than imitating; a firm with the same share that deliberately copies the leader and avoids provoking retaliation is a follower, so the label is set by chosen posture, not by size alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Strategy roleplays that hand you a share table expect the four positions named and the posture defended; calling every non-leader a competitor loses the distinction.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: Replacement time or space a medium owes when a commitment ran in the wrong position, ran late, or fell short of guaranteed delivery — a station that guarantees 150 gross rating points and delivers 120 owes those 30 points back as inventory, not as a cash refund.
terms.whyItMatters: An under-delivery roleplay tests whether the competitor asks for the right remedy; demanding money back where the contract promises replacement inventory usually forfeits the claim entirely.

terms.definition: Adding a product from a different category to the purchase — a case bought with a laptop — while upselling moves the customer up within the same line to a larger or higher-grade version of what they already chose. Suggestive selling covers both from the counter; the line that separates these two is category versus tier.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays scored on add-on sales ask you to name and demonstrate the technique, and calling a larger size a cross-sell is the error judges catch immediately.

terms.definition: An employee's pay divided by the midpoint of the assigned pay range, usually shown as a percentage: $52,000 against a $65,000 midpoint is 0.80, and $71,500 against the same midpoint is 1.10. Below 1.00 marks someone new or still developing in the job; a group average well under 1.00 across an experienced team is the standard signal that the range is being used to underpay.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-equity roleplays give a salary and a range and ask whether the person is paid fairly, which is answered with the compa-ratio and not with the raw dollar figure.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Optimizes the discounted value of a customer's entire future stream of purchases and will accept a thinner margin on any single sale to protect it, whereas transactional marketing maximizes margin on each separate exchange and budgets acquisition and retention as unrelated lines; the two approaches give opposite answers to whether a long-standing customer should be granted a concession on one order.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a loyal customer asks for an exception is decided by which of the two frames you argue from, and judges expect the alternative named.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: The FTC doctrine that an advertiser must already hold the evidence for an objective claim before that claim runs, and that health or performance claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence — the line separating a provable assertion from puffery, which makes no measurable claim and needs no proof.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants to advertise that a product works twice as fast is asking a legal question, and the competitor is scored on requiring the proof up front rather than promising to find it if challenged.

terms.definition: A written table stating how long each class of record is kept and when it must be destroyed, built on statutory floors rather than preference: the IRS's ordinary three-year assessment window, seven years for records supporting a bad-debt or worthless-securities claim, and the Sarbanes-Oxley requirement that audit work papers survive seven years.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-records roleplay asks how long the storeroom keeps signed invoices before shredding them, and a judge expects a statutory minimum, not a guess like 'a few years'.

terms.definition: Federal postal law lets anyone who receives goods they never ordered keep them as a free gift, with no duty to pay and no duty to ship them back, and a follow-up invoice creates no obligation. Only free samples plainly marked as such and merchandise sent by a charity asking for a donation fall outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items describe a company mailing a product with a bill attached and ask what the recipient owes; a customer-complaint roleplay expects you to tell the caller the item is theirs.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: A brand's own market share divided by the share of its single largest competitor — 20% against a leader's 40% is 0.5x, and only the market leader can score above 1.0 — which is the horizontal axis of the growth-share matrix; two brands holding an identical absolute share therefore land in opposite quadrants depending on how dominant the rival directly above each of them happens to be.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that reports 20% share and calls it strong is answered by asking what the leader holds; the ratio, not the raw percentage, is what drives the portfolio decision.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: The network of people and activities moving a product from raw materials to the customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain thinking underlies inventory, vendor, and cost decisions.

terms.definition: Coverage, mentions and shares a brand receives without buying placement — as against paid media, which is bought inventory the brand controls outright, and owned media, which is the brand's own site, list and channels. Only the paid third can be guaranteed to appear on a chosen date.
terms.whyItMatters: A launch-planning roleplay that leans on press pickup for a fixed launch day is the trap this term defends against, and public-relations items on the exam expect the three-way split to be named, not just the unpaid half.

terms.definition: The reason a customer buys from this particular seller — service, location, reputation, staff knowledge or credit terms — as distinct from the product motive, which is the reason they want the item from anyone at all. A rep losing on patronage grounds cannot recover the sale by describing the product better.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior exam items sort a list of customer statements into the two motive types, and a roleplay customer who says a competitor is closer to home is testing whether you answer with service instead of features.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: Holds that a firm should satisfy its target market's wants profitably only in ways that also preserve long-run consumer and social welfare — the third test the plain marketing concept leaves out — so an offering that customers genuinely want and the company profits from can still fail this standard because of the harm it does over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions that pit a profitable, popular product against a long-term harm are answered by naming this third test rather than by choosing between customers and profit.

terms.definition: Credential a private board grants after a psychometrically validated exam and keeps alive through periodic recertification, evidencing tested competence rather than legal permission. A certificate of completion is the near-neighbor that fools students: it is awarded merely for finishing a course, is never re-earned, and no board can revoke it.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on career-advancement resources ask which credential an employer will actually pay for; the answer is the one with an exam and a renewal cycle behind it.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: The share of a rebate offer's buyers who qualify but never file the paperwork, which is why a $50 mail-in rebate with 40% of buyers never claiming actually costs the manufacturer $30 per unit sold — the gap between a promotion's face value and its real cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing-and-promotion roleplay comparing an instant discount against a mail-in offer of the same face value turns on this: the two look identical to the customer and cost the manufacturer very different amounts.

terms.definition: A selling arrangement in which silence counts as a yes — the seller announces the coming shipment and bills unless the buyer declines in time. It is lawful only if the buyer agreed to the terms up front, gets at least 10 days to reject each announced selection, and can cancel through a route as simple as the one used to enroll.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a book or subscription club and ask what makes the automatic shipment legal; a subscription-selling roleplay is scored on disclosing the cancellation route before the customer signs.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: A concentration measure equal to the sum of the squared percentage market shares of every firm in a market — four firms at 25% each score 2,500 — where regulators treat readings above 2,500 as highly concentrated and scrutinize deals that raise the score by more than 200 points.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a share table and ask whether a merger would draw antitrust review, which requires squaring the shares rather than adding them.

terms.definition: Invitations sent per existing user multiplied by the share of those invitations that convert into new users — 5 invites at a 25% conversion rate gives k = 1.25 — where any value above 1.0 compounds into self-sustaining growth and any value below 1.0 produces a decaying series that halts on its own once paid acquisition stops, so the threshold is exactly 1.0 and not merely 'high'.
terms.whyItMatters: A referral-program roleplay is scored on stating the break-even threshold and the two inputs you would change to reach it, not on calling the campaign shareable.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: Paid placement built to match the form and feel of the surrounding editorial content, which the FTC requires be labeled Ad, Sponsored or Paid before the reader clicks — precisely because matching the publisher's format is what stops a reader from telling it apart from unpaid editorial.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay proposing an article that reads like the site's own reporting is scored on whether the competitor puts the disclosure ahead of the click, and exam items contrast it with publicity, which is unpaid and carries no label duty.

terms.definition: Guidance requiring any material connection between an endorser and a seller — payment, free product, a job, a family tie — to be disclosed clearly and right next to the claim rather than buried in a profile or behind a More link, and requiring a testimonial showing unusual results to state what a typical buyer should expect.
terms.whyItMatters: A social-selling roleplay that has you brief an influencer is graded on where the disclosure sits; exam items ask whether a free product with no cash payment still has to be disclosed, and it does.

terms.definition: The share of units clearing a step with no rework or scrap; multiplied across steps it gives rolled throughput yield, so four stations each at 95% deliver only 0.95^4 = 81.5% clean units, meaning a line whose every station reports 95% is really losing almost one unit in five.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality roleplays are scored on catching hidden rework: each station passing its own target while the finished-goods number falls short is exactly the scenario this calculation explains.

terms.definition: The break-even formula with the owner's desired profit added to the numerator: (fixed costs + target profit) / contribution margin per unit. Break-even sets that target to zero, so the answer here is always the larger of the two volumes for the same cost structure.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance judge asks not whether the store survives but how many units it must sell to fund a $30,000 owner's draw, which is this calculation rather than break-even.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: Environmental marketing claims the seller cannot substantiate, policed in the United States by the FTC's Green Guides at 16 CFR Part 260, which treat unqualified general claims such as 'eco-friendly' or 'green' as deceptive because they imply every possible environmental benefit, and require a degradability claim to mean complete breakdown within one year of customary disposal; a truthful narrow claim must therefore be stated narrowly to be lawful.
terms.whyItMatters: Sustainability roleplays that ask you to approve a packaging claim are scored on naming the standard and qualifying the claim, since an unqualified benefit statement is a legal exposure, not just a marketing choice.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Loyalty points, gift-card balances and promotional credits that were issued but are never redeemed and eventually release to revenue; a program booking 15% and then seeing only 5% has understated its outstanding liability threefold.
terms.whyItMatters: A loyalty-program roleplay asks whether a richer earn rate is affordable, and the answer depends on how much of what is issued is assumed never to be claimed — an assumption that turns into a balance-sheet problem when it is wrong.

terms.definition: Months a newly hired rep needs before carrying full quota, credited in steps — commonly no quota in the first quarter, half in the second and full in the third. A rep hired in March therefore contributes roughly a quarter of an annual number that year, which is why headcount added late almost never rescues a current-year gap.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items ask what revenue a mid-year hire adds this year, and the credit schedule is the whole answer; a roleplay on onboarding new sellers expects you to name the stepped quota rather than promise full production on day one.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: The same offering varies by employee, by customer, and by hour, so quality is a distribution rather than a specification; a factory good is held to a stated tolerance and any unit outside it is scrapped, while service variance has to be squeezed by scripts, training, and blueprints.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on internal service standards is scored on how you narrow the spread between your best and worst shift, not on restating that people differ.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: A written brief fixing one campaign's target, its single key benefit claim, the support that proves that claim, the tone of voice and the legal mandatories, so that every execution in every medium argues the same one thing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on why the pieces of a campaign must agree points here, and a roleplay presenting a campaign is expected to trace each execution back to the one claim the document fixed.

terms.definition: A business owned and run by two or more people who share profits and liabilities.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership law sets how partners share profits, decide, and bear business debts.

terms.definition: The sales-tax duty a seller picks up in a state where it owns no building and employs no one, triggered purely by volume — commonly $100,000 of sales or 200 separate transactions into that state in the current or prior year. Cross the threshold and the seller must register, collect and remit there; a purely online business is not exempt.
terms.whyItMatters: E-commerce selling items give a state-by-state sales table and ask where tax must now be collected; an expansion roleplay expects you to raise registration before recommending a push into a new state.

terms.definition: Sorts features into must-be, whose absence angers buyers while its presence earns nothing, performance features, where satisfaction rises with the amount delivered, and delighters, unnoticed when missing but thrilling when present -- and it predicts each delighter decays into a must-be as rivals copy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Feature-prioritization roleplays are scored on where to spend: pouring money into a must-be buys no preference, while the delighter that differentiates today becomes table stakes next season.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: Value created by converting raw materials into a finished good a buyer actually wants — wheat into bread, bauxite into a can — as distinct from place utility (moving the good to where the buyer shops), time utility (having it on hand at the hour demand occurs), and possession utility (transferring ownership through payment terms); a redesign adds form utility, a faster truck does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask how marketing adds value to a product are scored on naming which of the four utilities each activity creates and separating them; a general answer about 'adding value' loses the point.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: Sorts national communication styles into three categories rather than scoring dimensions: linear-active cultures (Germany, Switzerland, the U.S.) plan sequentially, do one thing at a time and argue from facts; multi-active cultures (Italy, Brazil, much of Africa) speak over one another, run several tasks at once and put the relationship ahead of the schedule; reactive cultures (Japan, China, Finland) listen first, do not interrupt, and answer only after a silence that outsiders misread as disagreement. Each country lands in one category, which is what makes it usable mid-meeting where a six-dimension score is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay in which the counterpart falls silent after your proposal is scored on reading the pause as a reactive-style norm instead of filling it with an unnecessary concession.

terms.definition: A prize promotion whose winners are drawn purely at random, which means it must strip one of the three elements of an illegal lottery — prize, chance and consideration — by publishing a free alternate method of entry so that no purchase is ever necessary.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants entries limited to paying customers is proposing an illegal lottery without realizing it, and the competitor is scored on naming the three elements and the free-entry fix rather than just calling it risky.

terms.definition: One deal's single commission pool divided between the rep who sourced it and the rep who closed it — 50/50, 30/70 or whatever the plan states — and the shares must total 100 percent. It changes who gets paid, never how much the company pays out, which is exactly the point students miss when they assume both reps earn a full commission.
terms.whyItMatters: Compensation items give a deal value, a commission rate and two named reps and check whether you double the payout; a team-selling roleplay expects you to settle credit before the sale, not after.

terms.definition: A process map drawn in horizontal bands split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility, and the line of internal interaction, so front-stage steps the customer sees sit above the backstage support that produces them, with failure points and wait times marked on the flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays that ask you to redesign a guest experience are scored on separating what the customer sees from the support behind it, which is where most delays actually live.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: Intangible activities that satisfy customer needs and wants.
terms.whyItMatters: Services require different quality, staffing, and marketing choices than goods.

terms.definition: Over-weighting a person's character and under-weighting their circumstances when explaining someone else's behavior — the late colleague is careless rather than stuck behind an accident. Its mirror image applied to oneself is the self-serving bias, and together the pair make an appraisal reward good luck and punish bad context.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why a supervisor rates a rep poorly after a territory loses its largest account expects this bias by name, and roleplays on fair evaluation reward asking about conditions before judging the person.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: An arrangement where a manufacturer reimburses part of a retailer's local advertising cost, usually on the condition that the ad features the manufacturer's brand and follows its format and logo rules, with reimbursement accrued against the retailer's purchase volume.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail roleplay where the store cannot afford a campaign alone is solved by claiming these funds, and the competitor is expected to name the strings attached rather than treat the money as unrestricted.

terms.definition: A municipal rule making uninvited door-to-door solicitation of a home unlawful, so a canvasser needs a local permit or an invitation from the occupant before knocking. Courts have upheld these ordinances, and violating one is an offense in that town even when the product, the price and the sales pitch are all perfectly legitimate.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items place a canvassing crew in a town with such an ordinance and ask what must happen first; a field-selling roleplay expects permits checked before a neighborhood route is planned.

terms.definition: The matrix that converts weighted customer wants into engineering specifications, scoring each intersection 9, 3, or 1 for a strong, moderate, or weak relationship, then ranking every specification by the sum of customer weight times relationship score to decide what engineering works on first.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-development roleplay that must justify which feature ships first is scored on tracing the choice back to weighted customer input rather than to engineering preference.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: What a sum invested today grows to by a stated date at a stated rate, computed forward with compounding rather than by adding equal yearly amounts.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-goal items give a monthly deposit and a rate and ask what the account holds in ten years; straight multiplication understates it.

terms.definition: Value added by making ownership transferable — credit terms, layaway, financing, leasing, the transaction mechanics themselves — rather than by making the good (form utility), delivering it to the buyer's location (place utility), or holding it until demand appears (time utility); a dealer that adds 60-month zero-interest financing changes the product's form, place, and time not at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and finance roleplays that ask you to justify offering a payment plan want the answer framed as a marketing utility the firm creates, not as a favor to the customer.
